title: small-payload-parse-queue-sampling-theory-wip
body:
Background:

Quick notes capturing an idea for why we're seeing elevated p99 CPU latency on small-payload requests even when GPU time is tiny. This is a brain-dump of measurement approaches, preliminary results, and an experimental plan. Not polished.

Problem statement:
- Production traces show many short requests (<= 64 tokens) with tail latency dominated by CPU-side work: parse/tokenize/queueing.
- GPU/Tensor time is ~1–3ms for these payloads, but end-to-end p95/p99 is 30–200ms.
- Hypothesis: threadpool handoffs, request parsing (JSON + header validation), and Python interpreter overhead (GIL + allocation patterns) amplify queuing and inflate tails when many small requests arrive together.

Observations from quick sampling (2025-02-10 smoke run):
- Agent-sampled stack traces (1000 samples across 5 hosts, 100 QPS burst) show repeated frames in:
  - json.loads -> _json.c: parse_loop
  - tokenizer.tokenize_sync -> pyx-layer
  - _threadpool.Queue.get -> blocking
  - tstate_lock_acquire -> ceval.c
- Median CPU parse time per-request ~ 6.2 ms (includes header parse, auth check, body decode). p99 parse time ~ 38ms.
- Avg threadpool queue depth during bursts: median 2, p99 18. Queue duration correlates with p99 tail.

Key ideas / working model:
1) Small request workload creates texture: many short-lived CPU tasks that are latency sensitive. If a worker is busy or blocked on Python-level GC or long tokenization, subsequent requests get queued -> non-linear tail growth.
2) Some tokenizers still call back into Python (hooked pre/post filters) which amplifies GIL contention.
3) JSON parse is single-threaded per-request and is a non-trivial portion for small payloads, especially with nested metadata.

Measurement plan (practical, low-cost telemetry):
- Lightweight per-request micro-metrics (emit via existing span headers):
  - parse_ms (split: header_parse_ms, body_decode_ms)
  - tokenize_ms (raw C tokenization vs python-wrapper overhead)
  - queue_wait_ms (time between accept and worker-start)
  - py_gil_hold_ms (sample-based estimate: fraction of sampling periods where thread is in a GIL-holding frame)
- Sampling approach: periodic 1kHz stack-sampler for 200ms windows when burst is detected; aggregate histograms at host-level and ship once per minute.
- Add a lightweight eBPF uprobe for json.loads hot path to measure C-level parse time without Python overhead.

Microbench harness outline:
- Controlled load generator: synthetic small payloads (2 sizes: tiny=8 tokens, small=32 tokens) with three variants of request shape:
  A) compact payload (minimal metadata)
  B) rich metadata (several headers, custom fields, longer JSON)
  C) auth-heavy (JWT verification simulated locally)
- Run isolated single-host tests to measure base CPU per-request, then ramp concurrency to measure queueing effects.

Preliminary experiment results (notes):
- Offloading tokenizer to rust-binding reduced median tokenize_ms from 4.8ms -> 1.1ms for small payloads, but overall p99 improvement was modest (25% at best) because JSON parse + queueing remained.
- Replacing json.loads with orjson improved body_decode_ms by 2–3x median, and reduced p95 by ~10ms under light load, but burst p99 still persisted.
- Increasing worker thread count reduces queue_wait_ms at low QPS but increases interference (more GIL acquisition events) and total CPU utilization; net win only when tokenizer is native and non-Python blocking.

Hypothesis refinement:
- Two dominant axis: per-request CPU cost (parse+tokenize) and variance (spiky long tail operations like auth verification, logging, or on-path caching misses). Both multiply in tail via queueing.
- Therefore optimizations need to reduce cost and variance. Reducing median alone won't fix tail if long-tail variance sources remain.

Suggested mitigations (ranked, quick to deploy -> more invasive):
1) Immediate (config):
  - Use orjson in hot path (low risk).
  - Tune threadpool size per host by workload; add autoscaling knob that considers p99 queue depth, not just CPU.
  - Disable non-critical Python hooks during high burst mode (feature flag).
2) Near-term (weeks):
  - Offload tokenizer to Rust extension and ensure tokenize path returns without Python callbacks (we saw good median improvements).
  - Introduce a pre-parse Nginx (or envoy) plugin to strip/validate headers for common formats so worker sees fewer heavy JSON fields.
  - Add a dedicated parse pool: a small set of pinned processes (processes, not threads) that only do JSON parsing and tokenization; use IPC (Unix socket) to return parsed AST to the worker. This reduces GIL competition because parser runs in separate interpreters/processes.
3) Longer-term (months):
  - Evaluate subinterpreters (PEP 554-style) or CPython MPM to reduce GIL impact on multi-threaded server.
  - Consider a hybrid model: acceptor process which does cheap validation, then route to specialized 'fast-path' worker processes that bypass Python where possible.

Telemetry items to implement ASAP:
- Histogram of queue_wait_ms per route/model (binned) shipped to console.
- Add parse_ms breakdown to request logs to allow root cause classification (parsing vs tokenization vs worker-scheduling).
- Alert: host-level p99(queue_wait_ms) > 50ms triggers runbook to reduce concurrency or enable fast-path.

Open questions / TODOs:
- How much of the long parse tail is external (e.g., KMS auth call / DB check)? We need trace spans for any external sync work.
- Can we instrument py-frame-based GIL hold time cheaply enough to run in prod? Marco is vetting a low-overhead sampler.
- Need to quantify cross-host variance: are tails localized to a few overloaded hosts or systemic? (Add per-host flamegraphs during burst).
- Evaluate memory allocation churn during parsing using jemalloc stats; does allocation pause cause GC-induced tail?

Action items (short tasks):
- [Liam] Add orjson import and run a canary on canary-hosts (INF-3124).
- [Aisha] Build microbench harness for small payloads and push results to infra-metrics.
- [Marco] Prototype process-based parse pool POC (use Unix sockets) and measure p99 improvements.
- [Team] Run 1-day burst-run with stack sampling and eBPF probes to collect representative data.

Notes to self and rough leads to include in the design doc:
- Important to separate API surface: "parse" vs "validate" vs "tokenize". Some customers rely on pre-parse validation side effects. Make fast-path opt-in per-model.
- Consider adding a prefix cache for frequently seen small prompts; prefix caching removes tokenization entirely for exact matches.
- Remember to avoid premature optimization: focus first on repeatable, instrumented wins (orjson, rust tokenizer) then move to process-level isolation.

References and links:
- Quick PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/987 (rust tokenizer binding)
- Jira ticket tracking telemetry work: JIRA-INF-3124
- Confluence skeleton: serving-runtime/request-parsing-metrics

Unresolved design concerns:
- Complexity cost of process-parse pool: introduces IPC latency and operational surface; need to ensure net tail reduction across workloads before committing.
- Feature toggles: we must be able to safely toggle fast-paths per-cluster and roll back rapidly.

End state goal:
- Reduce CPU-dominated p99 for small payloads to < 30ms across typical clusters by combining parse offload + median reductions + queueing-aware autoscaling.

If you read this and have immediate ideas (esp. about cheap GIL-hold sampling), ping me in #serving-runtime and tag Marco.

-- Liam
